passage: Tuition notes, Friday. Written by Eshaan, maths tutor. Chinmay, ten, taught me something this month. Two weeks ago I solved a whole fraction sum for him on the board. He copied it neatly and said "thank you" very softly, eyes on his slippers. The next day he couldn't do a single similar sum. Last week I swung the other way and gave him a page of word problems far past his level, then left him to it. Later he had drawn a cricket bat in the margin and written nothing. Today I sat near him with one problem that was hard but reachable. I asked what the question wanted, then waited. He got stuck twice, asked twice, and finished it. Then: "Can I do the next one alone?"

qa.q: What did Chinmay draw in the margin?
qa.a: A cricket bat.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's soft 'thank you', with his eyes on his slippers, suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seemed to feel quietly small, as if being handed the whole answer showed he couldn't do it himself.

qa.q: What did Eshaan change today, and why did it work?
qa.a: Eshaan gave one hard but reachable problem and stayed near, asking and waiting, so Chinmay could struggle, ask and finish it himself.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt facing the page of word problems alone?
qa.a: He likely felt lost and discouraged, which is why he drew instead of trying.

grounding: A tutor sees a boy learn nothing and feel small when handed the answer, give up when left with work far beyond him, and succeed with a hard task and help nearby.

passage: Dear Diary, Hemant bhaiya built my whole science model yesterday, the volcano with fizzing lava. Today Ma'am said it was the best in class and everyone clapped. I should have been happy. But when Ma'am asked how the lava works, I didn't know. I just stood there. My ears went hot. Then in the computer lab, sir gave us a game to code and was gone the whole period. I didn't know where to start, so I stopped trying and watched the clock. Tonight bhaiya asked if I wanted help with maths. I said, "Just sit next to me. Don't do it. Only tell me if I'm going wrong." We did three sums like that. The third one I got alone. - Raghav

qa.q: What model did Hemant bhaiya build?
qa.a: The volcano with fizzing lava.

qa.q: Why did Raghav's ears go hot when Ma'am asked how the lava works?
qa.a: Raghav felt embarrassed and small, because the praised model wasn't really Raghav's own work and Raghav couldn't explain it.

qa.q: What did Raghav ask for tonight, and why was it a turning point?
qa.a: Raghav asked bhaiya to sit nearby and only point out mistakes, and with that just-right help Raghav solved the third sum alone.

qa.q: How might Hemant bhaiya see his help differently after tonight?
qa.a: Hemant bhaiya may realise that building the whole model didn't help, while sitting beside Raghav without taking over did.

grounding: A child describes feeling small after too much help, giving up when left alone with too hard a task, and growing when a guide sits close without taking over.

passage: When the power came back in the evenings, Sangeeta, nine, sat on the veranda with her Kannada reader. Last week her older sister Gopika read every line aloud for her, fast, and Sangeeta only nodded, feeling smaller with each page. On Monday Gopika was busy with the cows and said, "Read chapter five alone." Sangeeta stared at the long words, shut the book and went to play in the lane. Tonight their Ajji sat down between them. "Gopika, read the first word only. Sangeeta, you do the rest." Sangeeta sounded out the next word slowly, then the next, getting stuck and asking. By the end of the page she was reading faster and grinning.

qa.q: What was Gopika busy with on Monday?
qa.a: The cows.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Gopika read every line aloud for her?
qa.a: She felt smaller with each page, since she only nodded while her sister did the reading.

qa.q: Which choice did Ajji make, and why did it help Sangeeta?
qa.a: Ajji had Gopika read only the first word and Sangeeta do the rest, giving just enough support for Sangeeta to keep going.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel seeing Sangeeta grinning at the end of the page?
qa.a: Gopika may feel pleased and a little surprised that doing less for her sister helped her read more.

grounding: A girl learns nothing when her sister reads everything, gives up when left alone with a hard chapter, and reads well when helped only at the start.

passage:
Priscila, ten, wanted to bake bread for the school fair in Porto Alegre, and her neighbour Jana was a baker.
The first Saturday, Jana did it all, flour, kneading, shaping, while Priscila held the spoon. The loaf was perfect. Priscila said thank you in a very small voice and didn't want to carry it.
The next Saturday Jana had a delivery. "You watched me. Try the braided one," she said, and left. The dough stuck to everything, the braid fell apart, and Priscila sat on the floor and cried.
The third Saturday Jana stayed, hands in her apron pockets. "What comes next, do you think?" When the braid sagged, she only said, "Tighter at the top." Priscila's loaf came out lopsided. She carried it to the fair herself.

qa.q: What did Priscila do while Jana did everything on the first Saturday?
qa.a: She held the spoon.

qa.q: Why did Priscila say thank you in a very small voice after the first loaf?
qa.a: She felt small because the perfect loaf wasn't really hers, which is why she didn't want to carry it.

qa.q: What changed on the third Saturday that finally worked?
qa.a: Jana stayed close but kept her hands in her pockets, asking questions and giving one tip, so the task was hard but not hopeless.

qa.q: What might Jana have noticed about Priscila across the three Saturdays?
qa.a: That doing everything and doing nothing both left Priscila unhappy, while standing by let her feel proud enough to carry her own loaf.

grounding: A girl feels small when a baker does everything, gives up when left alone with a hard loaf, and grows when the baker stays near with only a hint.

passage:
The chess club met in Room 12 on Wednesdays. Arnab Sir, the volunteer, handed Kalyani, nine, a thick puzzle book. "Checkmate in three. Start at page one." Then he went off to play the older boys.
Kalyani stared at the first board for ten minutes. Nothing made sense. Beside her, Manav flipped to the back. "Answers are here. Just copy." She copied four in neat pencil. When Arnab Sir came back and said, "Well done," her ears went hot and she shut the book.
The next Wednesday she said she had a headache and sat in the library.
The Wednesday after, Arnab Sir pulled a chair beside her with a smaller board. "Mate in one. I'll sit right here. Tell me what you see."

qa.q: Where did the chess club meet?
qa.a: It met in Room 12 on Wednesdays.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani's ears go hot when Arnab Sir said 'Well done'?
qa.a: She knew she had only copied the answers, so being praised for work that wasn't hers made her feel ashamed and small.

qa.q: What went wrong with the first puzzle book, and what did Arnab Sir change?
qa.a: He gave her puzzles far beyond her and walked away; later he sat beside her with a simpler mate-in-one and asked what she saw.

qa.q: How might Manav's shortcut look different from Kalyani's side than from Manav's?
qa.a: To Manav it was a helpful tip, but for Kalyani it turned a hard task into an empty one that left her feeling worse.

grounding: A girl left alone with chess puzzles far beyond her copies the answers, feels small and stays away, until the volunteer sits beside her with a reachable task.
